perm-005.title: Glossopteris forests rule the south
perm-005.text: Across the southern continents, one kind of tree came to dominate. Glossopteridales, an extinct order of seed plants, are known from the Permian of Gondwana. Once Gondwana had fused with Pangaea, glossopterid trees, chiefly Glossopteris, dominated large parts of the south. As glaciation waned in the Middle Permian, the Glossopteris flora flourished, and huge coal deposits formed from it, as in southern Brazil and Uruguay. These forests lasted until the end-Permian mass extinction, when they collapsed.

perm-006.title: The Gondwanide orogeny folds the south
perm-006.text: South Africa's Cape Fold Belt and Argentina's Sierra de la Ventana are the folded remains of one Permian mountain belt. Mountain building deformed southern Gondwana, in what are now southern South America, South Africa, Antarctica, Australia and New Guinea. Uplift linked to it split Brazil's Paraná Basin in two. In South Africa, folding entered a new phase from about 260 million years ago, after the ice sheets had melted and a great lake, the Karoo Sea, had spread.

perm-008.title: Lizards' ancestors part from the archelosaurs
perm-008.text: Lizards, snakes and their kin descend from a lineage called the Lepidosauromorpha. It is thought to have split from its sister group, the Archelosauria, during the Permian, a quiet fork in the reptile family tree with large consequences.

perm-013.title: Pangaea complete
perm-013.text:
In the Permian, almost every major landmass on Earth was part of a single continent. The supercontinent Pangaea stretched from the equator to both polar regions. Only parts of East Asia, such as Cathaysia, lay apart.

Gondwana's collision with the northern continents had completed most of it, leaving the Appalachian and Ouachita mountains near its center. The last pieces arrived during the Permian itself. Kazakhstania struck Baltica in the Cisuralian. Siberia joined in the late Permian, and North China, South China and Indochina fused with Pangaea by the period's end.

The supercontinent did not have long to enjoy its completion. Pangaea was complete roughly 20 million years before the end-Permian extinction. Its shape set the climate of the age: a single vast landmass spanning the globe, with an interior far from the sea, as {{ref:perm-014}} describes.

perm-014.title: The Pangean megamonsoon
perm-014.text: Pangaea's interior swung between parched months and violent rain. Permian climate was extremely seasonal, ruled by megamonsoons, giant seasonal wind systems that brought high aridity and harsh seasons inland. The monsoon shows in Permian rocks: Early Permian wind directions record a summer wet season. As the continents drifted north and spread more evenly across the equator, the megamonsoon grew stronger. Dryness alternating with seasonal rain became the normal climate across much of the continent.

perm-001.title: Aidaralash marks the start of the Permian
perm-001.text: In the Aidaralash River valley near Aqtöbe, Kazakhstan, a layer of rock marks the start of the Permian. The boundary is set by the first appearance of a conodont, Streptognathodus isolatus.

perm-007.title: Insects diversify into modern orders
perm-007.text: Most living insect orders arose during the Permian. Insects diversified dramatically in its early part, and those with complete metamorphosis radiated. Scorpionflies, true dragonflies and barklice first appeared. Older dominant groups faded: the palaeodictyopterans and giant griffinflies declined, and the palaeodictyopteran decline from the mid-Permian is linked to a change in plants. Insects and plants were already locked in an arms race, with insects chewing and plants evolving defenses.

perm-012.title: Cimmeria rifts away and the Neo-Tethys opens
perm-012.text: A strip of continent tore off Gondwana's northern edge in the Early Permian. Rifting broke away the Cimmerian blocks, including Sibumasu (Shan–Thai), Qiantang and Lhasa. As they drifted toward Laurasia, they closed the Paleo-Tethys ahead of them. Behind them opened a new ocean, the Neo-Tethys. It grew from a rift in what is now the Himalayan region and would dominate much of the Mesozoic.

perm-015.title: Patagonia completes its collision
perm-015.text: The Patagonian landmass had first touched south-western Gondwana in the mid-Carboniferous. In the early Permian came the broader collision. Deformation and metamorphism from it carried on into the Permian, welding Patagonia firmly to the supercontinent.

perm-017.title: Synapsids rule the land
perm-017.text: For some 40 million years, the dominant land animals were relatives of mammals. Pelycosaurs, early synapsids, peaked in the Cisuralian. Synapsids, the group that later gave rise to mammals, thrived and diversified greatly, quickly growing large. In North America and Europe, Early Permian faunas were led by plant-eating edaphosaurids and meat-eating sphenacodontids, alongside diadectids and amphibians. Pelycosaurs and their descendants, the therapsids, are the commonest land vertebrates in the best-known Permian fossil beds. A few pelycosaurs lingered late; the youngest known, from South Africa, is about 260 million years old.

perm-018.title: Kazakhstania meets Baltica and the Urals rise
perm-018.text: During the Cisuralian, the Kazakhstania block collided with Baltica. The collision belonged to the Uralian orogeny, which built the Ural Mountains during the Permian. Deformation carried on from the Carboniferous, and granites intruded the region extensively. The mountains mark the seam where these old continents were stitched into Pangaea.

perm-019.title: Carbon dioxide quadruples after a record low
perm-019.text: About 298 million years ago, carbon dioxide hit a record low. By 294 million years ago it had risen fourfold. Cooling had limited plant growth, and rising oxygen fed more fires; both returned carbon to the air, which reached about 300 ppm in the Permian. Rising seas drowned the coal swamps that had been burying carbon, so more stayed in the atmosphere and warmed the planet. By the Cisuralian, oxygen and carbon dioxide had returned to more normal levels.

perm-021.title: The Skagerrak large igneous province
perm-021.text: Magma spread over at least 0.5 million km² around today's Skagerrak strait, 297 ± 4 million years ago. This large igneous province reached the Oslo and Skagerrak grabens, south-western Sweden, Scotland, northern England and the central North Sea. It is the oldest of a series tied to the African superplume, a vast upwelling deep in the mantle, followed by Bachu, Emeishan, the Siberian Traps and the Central Atlantic. With Siberia's Barguzin-Vitim province, it is tied to the Moscovian and Kasimovian stages of the rainforest collapse, about 310–296 million years ago.

perm-022.title: The Central Pangean Mountains at their height
perm-022.text: In the early Permian, a mountain range along the equator rivaled today's Himalayas. The Central Pangean Mountains rose where Euramerica collided with northern Gondwana in the Variscan and Alleghanian orogenies, which began about 340 million years ago and ended about 295 million years ago. Their western part, the Appalachians, was uplifted then. The range cast a rain shadow that turned northern coal swamps into seasonally dry land and later helped lay down Europe's Zechstein salt. Weathering cut the peaks to about half their height by the Late Permian, spreading sandstone and conglomerate across Europe. The Appalachians, Ouachitas, Atlas and Bohemian Massif are its remnants.

perm-023.title: Dimetrodon appears
perm-023.text: The pelycosaur Dimetrodon evolved about 295 million years ago. Pelycosaurs like it diversified widely, and its remains turn up at Bromacker in Germany and in the Red Beds of Texas.

perm-024.title: The first beetles
perm-024.text: Beetles became one of the four great insect radiations, and they began near the start of the Permian, about 295 million years ago. By the Late Permian there were members of the Archostemata, the Adephaga and probably the Polyphaga, today the most diverse group of beetles.

perm-028.title: The Dobele crater
perm-028.text: An impact formed a crater 4.5 km across at Dobele, Latvia. Its age is about 290 ± 35 million years, in the Cisuralian. The wide margin of error leaves its place in the Permian story loose.

perm-029.title: The Panjal Traps erupt
perm-029.text: Lavas up to 2,500 m thick lie in Ladakh and Kashmir. They are the Panjal Traps, a large igneous province in what is now northwestern India, and zircons date them to 289 ± 2 million years ago. They may once have covered over 200,000 square km, comparable to the Emeishan Traps. The eruptions took place at about 33 degrees south and are tied to the opening of the Neo-Tethys Ocean, which carried the Cimmerian blocks away. Their lava chemistry shifts from continental types to ocean-floor types. Once linked to later extinctions, they are far too old; the Siberian Traps are the better candidate.

perm-030.title: The Artinskian warming melts the ice
perm-030.text: When the Permian began, the Late Paleozoic Ice Age was at its peak. It did not stay that way. Ice sheets shrank from the late Sakmarian on, and by 287 million years ago temperatures had risen and the south polar ice cap had retreated in the Artinskian Warming Event. Glaciers clung on only in eastern Australia's uplands. Around 285.1 million years ago, orbital cycles stopped driving ice growth and began driving marine anoxia and aridity instead, the turning point from icehouse to greenhouse. As the glaciers receded, seas rose and the continental interiors dried out.

perm-031.title: The Clearwater West crater
perm-031.text: Two craters sit side by side in Quebec, but they are not twins. Clearwater West, 36 km across, formed 286.2 ± 2.6 million years ago. Its neighbor, Clearwater East, is about 460–470 million years old, and different magnetic and meteorite signatures confirm separate impacts. Clearwater West is a complex crater: its central peak formed when the walls collapsed and the floor rebounded.

perm-032.title: The Choiyoi volcanic province
perm-032.text: Volcanic rock covers at least 200,000, and probably 500,000, square km of today's Argentina and Chile, 2–4 km thick. Subduction along Gondwana's western margin built this Choiyoi province from about 286 to 247 million years ago. Its rocks include lavas, breccias and rhyolitic ignimbrites, deposits of hot volcanic ash flows. During the Permian the volcanic arc migrated 350 km inland, reaching San Rafael about 280 million years ago. In Patagonia, late in the Permian, a sinking slab broke off and melted the crust above it. Choiyoi has been suggested as an additional cause of the end-Permian extinction.

perm-034.title: Mesosaurs and the oldest amniote embryos
perm-034.text: The earliest known amniote embryos come from the Mangrullo Formation of Brazil and Uruguay, of Artinskian age. The rocks are rich in mesosaurs. Mesosaurus fossils also occur in Permian black shales of Brazil's Paraná Basin, alongside Glossopteris coals.

perm-035.title: A late Kungurian cool spell
perm-035.text: Cooling resumed in the late Kungurian, bringing a cool glacial interval that lasted into the early Capitanian. Weathering of large igneous provinces from the Kungurian drew down carbon dioxide and brought on this P3 glaciation. Even so, temperatures stayed much higher than at the start of the Cisuralian, and in Australia the ice was largely alpine.

perm-038.title: The first Bennettitales
perm-038.text: Leaves from the Upper Shihhotse Formation of Shanxi, China, about 281 million years old, are the oldest confirmed bennettitalean fossils. The group stayed minor for a long time. It became a prominent part of floras only in the Late Triassic and held that place for much of the Mesozoic. Its oldest reproductive structures, the Williamsonia flowers, come from the Early Triassic of Australia.

perm-039.title: The Ternovka crater
perm-039.text: At Kryvyi Rih, Ukraine, a buried crater 11 km across records an impact about 280 ± 10 million years ago, in the Early or Middle Permian.

perm-040.title: Coconino dunes cover the Grand Canyon region
perm-040.text: The pale cliffs of the Coconino Sandstone in the Grand Canyon are fossil sand dunes. About 275 million years ago the region dried out, and quartz sand spread across a growing desert. Wind piled it into large cross-bedded dunes, now famous for trackways of scorpion-like arthropods and early tetrapods. Deserts seem to have been widespread on Pangaea, whose interior was dominated by dunes and evaporites.

perm-041.title: The first therapsids
perm-041.text: Therapsids, the synapsid line leading to mammals, split from pelycosaur-grade synapsids around 275 million years ago. Their earliest history is missing. No confirmed therapsid fossils come from the Early Permian, leaving a long ghost lineage, a stretch of time a group must have existed without leaving fossils. Raranimus, from the early Middle Permian of China, is probably the earliest-diverging therapsid known. Accounts differ on when all the major therapsid groups had appeared: by 275 million years ago, or by 265 million years ago in the Wordian.

perm-043.title: Ceratitid ammonoids appear
perm-043.text: Ceratitid ammonoids arose in the Middle Permian from the daraelitid family of prolecanitids. Barely touched by the Capitanian extinction, they radiated to dominate Late Permian ammonoids as the goniatitids declined. They went on to include almost all Triassic ammonoid genera.

perm-045.title: Reefs peak and the Capitan Reef rises
perm-045.text: Texas's Capitan Formation, curving around the Delaware Basin, is called the world's best-preserved Paleozoic reef complex. It may have risen 61–91 m above the seafloor. Reef building peaked in the Guadalupian, with reefs abundant from the Delaware and Zechstein basins to the Tethys and cool Panthalassa shelves. The Capitan Reef was built mainly by calcareous sponges and encrusting algae, not corals, and brachiopods were key ecosystem engineers. Its end came from geography. Tectonics restricted the Hovey Channel, rising heat and salinity killed the reef, and brines laid down the Castile Formation evaporites.

perm-047.title: Therapsids take over from the pelycosaurs
perm-047.text:
As the Permian world grew drier, the land changed hands. Therapsids replaced pelycosaurs as the dominant large land animals in the Guadalupian, and they kept that role into the Early Triassic.

How the takeover unfolded is hidden. A poor fossil record across Olson's Gap leaves the transition mostly unseen. What follows it is clear. Giant dinocephalians, both plant-eaters and meat-eaters, dominated Middle Permian faunas of South Africa and Russia. Therocephalians arose and took over the role of saber-toothed predator.

Those two regions share animals for a reason. Coastal swamp corridors along East Pangaea let animals migrate between what are now South Africa and Russia. The therapsids would go on to produce {{ref:perm-060}}, the line that eventually led to mammals.

perm-046.title: Sea level falls to a Paleozoic low
perm-046.text: Through the Early Permian, the sea stood several tens of meters higher than today. A sharp fall began in the Roadian and reached the lowest level of the whole Paleozoic, near today's, in the Wuchiapingian. This Permian regression may be tied to the formation of Pangaea. Falling seas, rising carbon dioxide and a worsening climate marked the Lopingian, ending in the end-Permian extinction.

perm-048.title: Olson's Extinction
perm-048.text: Most pelycosaur lineages vanished around 273 million years ago, long before the end-Permian crisis. Edaphosaurids and ophiacodontids died out near the Kungurian–Roadian boundary, while caseids and therapsids diversified. Temnospondyl amphibians declined sharply afterward, and extinction rates in fish rose. Extreme environments in Kansas, combining heat and acidic waters, coincide with it, pointing to climate change as a possible cause. This proposed extinction is contested. A review of Kungurian and Roadian beds found the turnover real, but some authors argue it reflects poor sampling or gradual change, and the timing of Olson's Gap is disputed.

perm-050.title: Saber-toothed gorgonopsians appear
perm-050.text: Inostrancevia reached 3.5 m long and about 300 kg, with saber teeth. It belonged to the gorgonopsians, which first evolved about 270 million years ago and lasted until about 252 million years ago. They started small, with skulls 10–15 cm long. The oldest identifiable one, Phorcys, dates to about the Wordian–Capitanian boundary, though finds show the group was already diversifying earlier in the Wordian. Once the Capitanian extinction removed the dinocephalians, gorgonopsians became the apex predators.

perm-051.title: The Hunter–Bowen orogeny
perm-051.text: About 2,500 km of eastern Australia's margin was crumpled by island arcs colliding with it in the Permian and Triassic. Pangaea's counterclockwise rotation drove sideways squeezing along the subduction zone there. A megafold had formed earlier, around 290 million years ago. Major contraction came about 270–260 and around 253 million years ago, with a later phase about 235–230 million years ago. In front of the mountains, the Sydney–Bowen basins filled with sediment that built vast coal deposits.

perm-055.title: A cooling recorded in carbon
perm-055.text: Marine limestones of Capitanian age record a rise in carbon-13, the heavier form of carbon, a sign of global cooling. That cooling may have caused the end-Capitanian extinction of warm-water species: large fusulinids, alatoconchid bivalves and waagenophyllid rugose corals.

perm-056.title: The Capitanian mass extinction
perm-056.text: About 60–63% of marine species died out at the close of the Middle Permian. The Capitanian extinction began around 262 million years ago and peaked around 259 million years ago. It took about 33–35% of marine genera. Ammonoids, corals, reef algae, foraminifera, bryozoans and brachiopods suffered most. On land, the dinocephalians and the last varanopids vanished, and anomodont diversity halved. It is linked to {{ref:perm-057}}, which drove two ocean anoxic events and acidification, and to a sea-level fall that killed reefs. How severe and how global it was is still debated. Some rank it fifth worst ecologically; others see only a regional crisis in South China, or losses limited to low-latitude northern species.

perm-057.title: The Emeishan Traps erupt
perm-057.text: In south-western China, basalt covers more than 250,000 km², up to 5.5 km thick, an estimated 300,000 km³ in all. These Emeishan Traps began erupting 265 million years ago or earlier, peaked between 262 and 261 million years ago, and ended about 259 million years ago. They had global ecological impact and are tied to the Capitanian extinction, though the later Siberian Traps dwarfed them. Around 260 million years ago they caused the Emeishan Thermal Excursion, a warm interruption of a cool period. Afterward, weathering of the basalts drew down carbon dioxide and cooled the early Wuchiapingian. Coronene at the boundary, with no iridium anomaly, points to volcanism rather than an impact.

perm-060.title: The first cynodonts
perm-060.text: Cynodonts, the therapsid group ancestral to mammals, first appeared in the Late Permian, about 260 million years ago, and spread worldwide. The earliest known, Charassognathus, comes from the Wuchiapingian. They are the only major therapsid group with no Middle Permian record. Their big moment came later: they diversified rapidly after the end-Permian extinction.

openers.permian-period: In the Permian, almost every major landmass was gathered into one supercontinent, Pangaea. Its climate was extremely seasonal, ruled by megamonsoons that brought harsh dry seasons to the interior. In the south, mountain building folded Gondwana from South America to New Guinea, and Glossopteris seed plants spread across the land. Among the reptiles, the lineage leading to lizards split from its sister group.
openers.cisuralian-epoch: The Cisuralian, the first Permian epoch, opened in the grip of an ice age and ended in a warming world. Carbon dioxide hit a record low and then rose fourfold within a few million years. Pelycosaurs such as Dimetrodon were the dominant land animals, insects diversified dramatically, and the first beetles appeared. Meanwhile the map kept shifting: Kazakhstania struck Baltica, Patagonia completed its collision, and the Cimmerian blocks broke away from Gondwana.
openers.guadalupian-epoch: The Guadalupian, the Middle Permian, was a time of reefs and new predators. Reef building peaked, with reefs from the Delaware Basin to the Tethys. On land, therapsids replaced pelycosaurs as the dominant large animals, and saber-toothed gorgonopsians evolved. The epoch ended in crisis, as the Emeishan flood basalts erupted in China and the Capitanian extinction struck.

reviews.permian-period: The Permian's big picture is one continent and one harsh climate. Pangaea, stretching from pole to equator, created the megamonsoon that swung its interior between drought and rain. In the south, the Gondwanide mountains rose and Glossopteris forests spread, building coal as the ice waned. Among the animals, quiet splits such as that of the lizard lineage set up the reptile world to come.
reviews.cisuralian-epoch: The Cisuralian turned an icehouse into a greenhouse. After carbon dioxide hit its record low, it rose again as drowned coal swamps stopped burying carbon, and the Artinskian warming melted most of the southern ice. Pangaea gained its last pieces as Kazakhstania met Baltica and the Urals rose, while volcanic provinces from Skagerrak to Panjal and Choiyoi erupted. On land, pelycosaurs ruled and deserts such as the Coconino dunes spread, while insects and beetles diversified and the first therapsids split off.
reviews.guadalupian-epoch: The Guadalupian's peaks and its ending are linked. Reefs reached their height, from the Capitan Reef of Texas outward, and therapsids such as dinocephalians took over the land after Olson's Extinction. Then sea level fell, the climate cooled, and the Emeishan Traps erupted, together driving the Capitanian extinction. Its losses opened the way for gorgonopsians as top predators and for ceratitid ammonoids, while the first cynodonts appeared soon after.
